item.description: Stolen merchandise passes through two layers of hands: boosters are recruited to steal from stores, and fences clean off the identifiers and resell, after which the goods go up on secondhand platforms. Networked goods fetch 70-80% of retail; T-shirts and deodorant only 30-something percent.
item.content:encoded:
Stolen merchandise passes through two layers of hands: boosters are recruited to steal from stores, and fences clean off the identifiers and resell, after which the goods go up on secondhand platforms. Networked goods fetch 70-80% of retail; T-shirts and deodorant only 30-something percent.

High information density: Home Depot's head of asset protection breaks down how shrink is categorized, the real P&L of locking up shelves, the pricing patterns of stolen goods, and the progress of federal legislation — lots of hard numbers.

8:19 A third of shrink is self-inflicted
Home Depot splits shrink into two buckets: operational/administrative and malicious — in Scott's phrasing, the things we do to ourselves versus the things others do to us. At Home Depot, about 30% of shrink falls into the former, with the rest on the malicious side. The industry line that has circulated for years: of malicious shrink, about 40% is caused by internal employees, 35% by people who walk into the store, and the remainder is self-inflicted operational shrink. These percentages move only within a few points each year, but he thinks they are drifting upward, and that it has been underreported ever since COVID — neither police reports nor the FBI's Uniform Crime Report fully capture it.

22:52 Employees are explicitly told not to chase anyone
The bigger problem isn't money, it's people. Scott says professional criminals often use homeless people and addicts to go into stores and steal; these people have one thing on their minds — getting the goods out to trade for money — so they will fight, and they have fought. People have been injured in Home Depot stores, and people have been killed. So asset protection staff are trained in de-escalation, and the 400,000 store employees are explicitly told not to intervene — just back off. His attitude: he would trade shrink for human safety every single day, and management and the board would back that decision.

23:53 RFID dies the moment it enters a steel store
Joe asks why RFID has been talked about for 25 years and is still expensive and hard to scale in 2026. Scott says he doesn't understand it either, but explains Home Depot's particularity: it's a hardware store, and the store is full of steel, essentially a Faraday cage, so passive RFID can't be read — you can only use solutions that actively transmit a signal. He also says tag cost is now almost zero; the real bottleneck is the reading hardware — covering a 140,000-square-foot sales floor with eight separate entrances and exits is extremely costly. They've tried the idea of bricking merchandise before it leaves the store, but to do that for a single drill you'd have to rework an entire production line, and it's very hard to scale.

25:58 Stolen goods have been pushed onto secondhand platforms
The division of labor works like this: boosters are recruited and given a list, cash, or the promise of drugs, and go steal from stores; the goods go to a fence — maybe a garage, a warehouse or a flea market — who strips the price tags, store labels and electronic tags before reselling, and the money flows up to whoever runs the operation, which might be a small crew of a few people or a transnational gang. After the INFORM Act took effect in 2023, big platforms like Amazon and eBay were required to verify seller identities, so stolen goods shifted to Craigslist and Facebook Marketplace, because the law left a gap that doesn't cover peer-to-peer sellers. Home Depot works backward from the platforms, using models to flag sellers pricing below cost while moving large volumes.

35:19 One combo kit sold means restocking 4.2 times
Whether to lock up shelves is a financial question. Scott says they look at the data: there's a combo kit priced at $799, and for every one sold, they have to restock 4.2 times. Take that to finance and they immediately get that it's a gross margin problem — as long as it breaks even or even makes a little, locking it up pencils out. But half of Home Depot's revenue comes from professional contractors, and if they break a bit on the job site, rush to the store and find it out of stock, that's a loss too. So they lock up a carefully selected set of categories, with a QR code to summon an associate, and the average unlock takes 90 seconds; locking things up doesn't necessarily hurt sales — in some categories sales actually rose, because the product was finally in stock.

39:23 A fake bill of lading can just drive the goods away
In the supply chain he counts three plays: first, pure diversion — a whole container is rerouted at the port or a transload warehouse and driven elsewhere, even loaded back onto a container ship and shipped away; second, a driver drives eight hours across state lines, and while he sleeps someone pries open the trailer doors and moves boxes; third, forged bills of lading and pickup orders, made to look real with AI, and a driver pulls in, says he's picking up a certain trailer, and just drives off. He says what's new isn't necessarily the methods, it's the volume, because these cases are very hard to pursue. Rail is the area that has clearly worsened over the past five or six years — cars sitting in a yard get pried open by a group; and their intelligence is good, they don't touch every car, only the one carrying guns or electronics.

41:28 In security, AI is an efficiency tool
Scott says they have more cases than they can investigate, so for them AI is an efficiency question: a typical organized retail crime case takes an average of 70 days from discovery to closure and handoff to police, and compressing that cycle means they can work more cases. They just replaced the video management system across all 2,300 stores, letting existing cameras run edge analytics — identifying people who linger too long in an area, deliberately avoid associates, or show up where they shouldn't be. He also admits that to identify a particular combination of suspicious behaviors and then recognize the specific person, he doesn't have enough cameras yet, but they will get there. Separately, they have an in-house company doing web scraping.

44:30 Seven years ago nobody cared; now there's a federal bill
He says he's very optimistic now. INFORM is arguably the first federal bill driven by organized retail crime, and next is CORCA (Combating Organized Retail Crime Act): the retail industry broadly supports it, it has bipartisan cosponsors, it has passed the House, it's attached to the NDAA awaiting Senate passage, and the president has said he'll sign it. The rationale is that this crime is inherently interstate — it happens in Cobb County, Georgia, and the goods flow to South Carolina and North Carolina, which is interstate transportation of stolen property, but there were no corresponding federal resources; the bill would provide resources, prosecutors and a coordination center. Seven years ago he was thoroughly pessimistic about this: nobody took it seriously, and the prevailing mood then was decriminalization and defunding the police.

item.title: Making Your Rivals Depend on Your System Is How America Has Won for Three Centuries

item.description: The Dutch, the British and the Americans took turns as hegemon not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake their survival on someone else's maritime order — once they can't live without the sea lanes and the markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective weapon short of war.
item.content:encoded:
The Dutch, the British and the Americans took turns as hegemon not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake their survival on someone else's maritime order — once they can't live without the sea lanes and the markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective weapon short of war.

Walter Mead breaks America's three-century winning streak into a five-step strategy and pushes it all the way to China, the Taiwan Strait and AI deterrence. What you get is a durable framework for judgment, not news-cycle opinion.

4:47 Unpredictability is a form of power
‘Unpredictability’ is not madness; it is a modern strategy of power. Mead says post-Cold War American diplomacy held itself up as a pillar of stability by ‘letting the whole world know where America's red lines are’, while Trump profits by doing the opposite: crossing lines, threatening allies, turning commitments into bargaining chips. He saw through a secret of the information age — the marginal cost of lying: the first lie is expensive, the thousandth is nearly free. When Clinton was engulfed by the Lewinsky scandal, he discovered that shame only lives in other people's minds; as long as you keep walking, the dogs bark but the caravan moves on. Trump took that insight to industrial scale. The cost is borne by the American diplomatic system: when the world's number one power turns itself into the unpredictable card, every alliance and rule built on predictability after World War II is coming apart faster.

10:00 The last step of global hegemony is cutting the cord
The Anglo-American maritime order did not win through some battle; it won through a five-step playbook. First, an open society on an island — the 17th-century Dutch tolerated heretics and Jews, and ideas and capital poured in. Then global trade: Dutch merchant ships went everywhere, and the wealth was so great that even the paintings are full of Turkish carpets and Brazilian parrots. Third, while continental powers fought over inland Silesia, you seized India and Canada across the globe. The fourth step is the riskiest: instead of copying Spain and sealing off your colonies, you invite the whole world in to do business, the British navy suppresses pirates, and every merchant ship benefits; Germany and Japan were likewise invited in after the war. Only the last step is the hole card: once the other side cannot live without your grain, your rubber and your shipping lanes, you cut it off — Germany discovered in World War I that Argentine grain and Malayan rubber had all been cut off, and its economy collapsed immediately.

16:38 Everything China does is to avoid having its umbilical cord cut
Look at China through the same framework and you find Beijing is well aware of its own vital point. Mead says: suppose the mainland blockades Taiwan, and the US counter-blockades from a hundred miles off Taiwan's coast — oil cannot get in, manufactured goods cannot get out, soybean contracts with Brazil and Argentina are voided, and China's economy is strangled alive. He has discussed these things with officials and scholars at Chinese universities, and this worry is always present. So China's energy policy has to be read side by side: on one hand building oil reserves so large they surprise outsiders; on the other, throwing up solar and hydropower while digging as much coal as possible. It is not schizophrenia, it is the same thing: pulling out the soft spots of ‘dependence on the outside world’ one by one. He also warns the US not to retreat into isolationism — agriculture and AI both need overseas markets to keep themselves alive.

25:50 Every round of technological bounty needs a new institution to match
Mead starts from the ownership society: at America's founding there were independent farmers with land everywhere, and while a bridge is nice it raises my taxes — that trade-off is itself a political education. The railroad era was matched by the Homestead Act, with the government giving land to railroad companies and farmers, and a national market grew out of it; in the 20th century what replaced the family farm was the single-family suburban house, paired with tax-exempt municipal bonds and highways, becoming a new machine for distributing wealth. Now that machine has hit housing prices: young people cannot afford to live near where they work. His remedy is remote work and autonomous driving. When the commuting radius expands from 40 miles to 75 miles, usable land for housing rises with the square of the radius, and the physical space opened by technology is enough to carry two more generations. But the precondition is filling in the institutional ‘infrastructure’ — he coined the word info-structure, meaning the institutions and regulatory rules that let AI actually land in hospitals and courts.

40:22 Silicon Valley tilts toward the tech Hamiltonians
American foreign policy debate has for centuries been four vocabularies: Hamiltonians want a strong state to clear the way for capital, Wilsonians want to spread liberal democracy, Jeffersonians fear a bigger government, and Jacksonians stay isolationist in peacetime and fight to the death when hit. The post-Cold War establishment was a marriage of Hamilton and Wilson, but Trump brought Jefferson and Jackson into the room. Mead says the new species truly worth noting is the Tech Hamiltonian. In the 1990s tech companies loved to say ‘we are a global company, Google has no borders, Washington has no say’; AI competition has turned tech into a contest of national destiny. Economic positions changed too: the old multinational car companies wanted borderless labor and markets, while Silicon Valley wants supply chain and IP security, and even wants its employees to be patriotic — selling code to China is shameful, and your colleagues will report you outright. The core of business has shifted from the old multinationals to tech nationalists, and this is the underwater current of America's political realignment.

50:00 The power with more equipment fears technological turnover most
Mead has been to Ukraine twice. The first time he went to a drone factory and saw them converting children's toy trucks into ground drones carrying mines to blow up tanks; months later he went again and the progress was unimaginably fast. The battlefield is now a gray kill zone, usually only two or three soldiers move together, and one of the hardest problems is ‘how to get the wounded out’ — you need to build a ground drone with a metal shield to drag people, with a squad of drones alongside hunting the enemy drones coming to attack. He heard of one wounded soldier who took 63 days to be evacuated from the front. The changes flip every six months. The bitterest irony for the US: the power with the most tanks and aircraft carriers is precisely the one most afraid of this kind of parameter revolution — existing equipment turns from an advantage into a relocation cost. Russia's Black Sea Fleet has no great battle to fight, yet it is bottled up at home by Ukrainian small boats and drones.

54:16 The new variable most worth watching in the Taiwan Strait is Japan
On ‘will the mainland attack Taiwan’, Mead's judgment is that Beijing needs a very high probability of success before it is willing to cross the threshold — once it fails, it is catastrophic for the initiator. But between ‘attack’ and ‘do nothing’ there is a long gray ladder: for example, requiring all merchant ships bound for Taiwan to stop first at mainland ports for customs clearance, or imposing a soft blockade — actions sufficient to change facts on the ground without triggering an armed US response. The real new variable on the Taiwan board is not America's attitude but Japan. The Japanese have already publicly concluded that if China takes Taiwan, Japan's independence is finished too; they are raising defense budgets, rewriting security doctrine, reshaping the national psyche. Historically Japan turns very fast when faced with a real threat. How steep Japan's learning curve is, and whether Beijing's calculations must factor Japan in, is the key to the Taiwan question in the coming years.

1:10:00 AI actually makes deterrence more credible
Moving Cold War deterrence logic into the algorithmic age, Mead points to a counterintuitive corollary: deterrence succeeds or fails on making the opponent one hundred percent believe ‘if I do X, you will necessarily do Y, and you can do it and are willing to’. As long as there is a human veto point in the decision chain — ‘I might soften when the time comes’ — that commitment has a crack. Automating part of foreign policy decision-making with AI amounts to turning retaliation into an executable mechanism that will not hesitate — deterrence becomes more credible. But this is the doomsday machine problem from science fiction: decisions of civilizational scale no longer require a human to bear the consequences. His own assessment of the question is ‘very interesting and a little confusing’, and he does not think the answer has appeared yet.

item.title: ECT Is Not What You Think: A Century of Drift from Back Room to Routine Treatment
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-tpwky-ect-不是你想的那样-从密室到常规治疗的百年漂移/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-tpwky-ect-不是你想的那样-从密室到常规治疗的百年漂移/
item.description: Modern ECT is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with strong efficacy, but the evidence on memory-loss side effects remains incomplete, and social misunderstanding has left it over-stigmatized.
item.content:encoded:
Modern ECT is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with strong efficacy, but the evidence on memory-loss side effects remains incomplete, and social misunderstanding has left it over-stigmatized.

If your image of ECT is still stuck on One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, this episode will reset it entirely. Hear the actual procedure, the indications, the side effects, and one expert's clinical account.

8:07 The actual ECT procedure, step by step
If you or I were to receive ECT, here is how it goes: first a risk assessment and informed consent, then a physical exam, then an overnight fast. The next morning, in a hospital or outpatient setting, an IV line is placed along with two blood pressure cuffs (arm and right leg), and EKG, EEG and EMG leads are connected. After the anesthesiologist puts you to sleep, the leg cuff is inflated to restrict blood flow to the right foot, then a muscle relaxant such as succinylcholine is given. Once the muscles are fully relaxed, a bite block is placed, and then a brief pulse of current is delivered through the electrodes (lasting seconds, or even half a second). The goal is not to make your whole body convulse, but to induce a generalized seizure, typically lasting 25-70 seconds. Because the muscles are already relaxed, you see almost no external movement — the whole thing is obvious on the EEG.

14:15 Electrode placement, and why the right side comes first
There are several electrode placements: bitemporal (the way it looks in the movies), bifrontal, and most commonly 'right unilateral' — one electrode on the right temple, the other on the right side of the top of the head. Right unilateral is used for most people because it produces fewer cognitive side effects. Why consider the right side first? Because for about 98% of right-handed people and 70%-90% of left-handed people, language function sits in the left temporal lobe. Avoiding electrical stimulation on the left side theoretically reduces language-related memory problems. But right unilateral is slightly less effective than bilateral. During a course of treatment, doctors switch based on side effects and efficacy: if bilateral side effects are too heavy, switch to right unilateral; if right unilateral is not working well enough, switch to bilateral.

16:20 Seizure threshold and the effective dose
The seizure threshold is the minimum amount of current that can induce a seizure. There is no precise measuring device, so you start by estimating from age, then titrate upward from a low dose until a seizure appears. But treatment does not stop at merely reaching threshold — the effective dose is usually 2.5 to 5 times the threshold. With bilateral, 2.5 times is enough, whereas right unilateral needs 5 times, because unilateral stimulation has a harder time achieving the same effect. The dose varies from person to person and has to be adjusted as you go. If in one session a patient's seizure does not occur or does not last long enough (under 25 seconds), the doctor may increase the dose and try again. Treatment is generally three times a week, with a full course of 6 to 18 sessions, sometimes longer.

20:22 We still do not know exactly how ECT works
Why does passing electricity through the brain treat depression and catatonia? Frankly: we still do not fully understand. There are several leading hypotheses. One is neurotransmitter change: after ECT, serotonin, dopamine and GABA (an inhibitory transmitter) all shift markedly. The rise in GABA is itself anticonvulsant, which could explain why the seizure threshold rises and seizures get shorter over a course of treatment. Two, large fluctuations in hormones such as ACTH, prolactin and TSH are seen in the hypothalamus and pituitary. Three, ECT promotes neurogenesis, with BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) as a key molecule. But how these changes directly relieve symptoms still has no one-to-one mechanism. Different illnesses (depression, schizophrenia, catatonia) may also work through different mechanisms, and for now the only option is to keep researching.

24:24 Depression data: far better than first-line antidepressants
For treating severe depression, ECT's key numbers are quite strong: most studies report remission rates (symptoms fully gone) of 50%-60% and response rates (symptoms clearly improved) of 60%-90%. By comparison, the best remission rate for SSRI antidepressants is only about 40%. ECT has another uncommon benefit — it can cut the 30-day readmission rate in half. This is not to say it should be first choice, nor that it has no risks (relapse or symptom rebound within 6-12 months is still not rare); but in patients with treatment-resistant depression combined with severe suicide risk, these efficacy advantages are hard to ignore.

26:27 Among side effects, memory problems draw the most concern
ECT's most difficult side effects center on cognition and memory. Right after the procedure there is a brief period of confusion lasting from a few dozen seconds to half an hour, and for weeks there may be declines in attention and executive function. Interestingly, most cognitive function actually improves in the long term — possibly because the depression improves. The real trouble is memory. Anterograde amnesia (difficulty forming new memories) usually recovers within a few weeks after the course ends, which is why many people are restricted from driving or making major decisions during treatment. Retrograde amnesia (losing past memories) is what worries patients more: it typically affects recall of the most recent months or even years before treatment, and in most cases recovers, but in some portion it is permanent. Bilateral treatment is more prone to this problem than right unilateral.

34:55 Catatonia: a frequently misread, fatal syndrome
Catatonia is often simply lumped in as a subtype of schizophrenia, but it is actually a psychomotor syndrome that any psychiatric or neurological illness can trigger. Patients appear awake, eyes open, yet are almost completely immobile and mute; they may show posturing or waxy flexibility (an arm placed in a position stays there). Because they cannot eat or drink and do not move for long periods, they are prone to malnutrition, pressure sores, muscle contractures, and even death. Untreated catatonia has a mortality rate as high as 20%! The most common treatment is benzodiazepines, but ECT is extremely effective in catatonia from many causes. The girl with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis mentioned earlier (the 'Brain on Fire' case) developed catatonia; immunotherapy and lorazepam both failed, and she ultimately recovered with ECT.

48:36 The biggest bottleneck is not efficacy but access
Dr. Lopez believes the biggest obstacle ECT faces today is finding a place to get it. His hospital performs more than 6,000 treatments a year across two campuses, averaging about 10-12 sessions per patient. But it is not widely available across the United States, and adults and children traveling across state lines for care are not few — especially in infants, children and adolescents with catatonia from autoimmune encephalitis, where finding an experienced treatment team is extremely hard. Improving access is therefore his greatest hope. At the same time, doctors on other internal medicine, pediatric and critical care teams often do not recognize catatonia and do not dare, or do not think, to call an ECT consult; so 'preaching' to non-psychiatric colleagues is part of his daily work.
