item.description: From refusing to salute the flag to having a purse searched, six cases gradually drew the constitutional rights of American public school students; the Supreme Court laid down that "schools are not totalitarian enclaves" while accepting that corporal punishment and reasonable-suspicion searches do not violate the Constitution, and the boundary of those rights narrowed accordingly.
item.content:encoded:
From refusing to salute the flag to having a purse searched, six cases gradually drew the constitutional rights of American public school students; the Supreme Court laid down that "schools are not totalitarian enclaves" while accepting that corporal punishment and reasonable-suspicion searches do not violate the Constitution, and the boundary of those rights narrowed accordingly.

Each case gets five or six minutes laying out the background and the holding, suited to listeners who want to grasp in one sitting where the lines fall on speech, corporal punishment and searches in American public schools.

5:10 The flag-salute case: student rights enter the schoolhouse for the first time
Can students really invoke the First Amendment in class? This case actually begins with religion: Jehovah's Witnesses families held that saluting the flag violated the commandments against having other gods and against graven images, and refused to pledge or salute the flag. In 1940 the Supreme Court had ruled against them, and World War II pushed more school districts to require students to salute and recite the pledge daily. West Virginia expelled students who refused the pledge, classified them as delinquents, and their parents could be fined or even jailed. In 1943 the Supreme Court overturned the earlier ruling 6 to 3, and Justice Jackson wrote the opinion on Flag Day: orthodoxy in politics, nationalism, religion or other matters of opinion is not to be defined by any official; students need not utter words they do not believe or make hollow gestures. This was the first time the Court established that students hold some First Amendment rights inside school.

11:21 An official prayer text is held unconstitutional
In the Cold War the United States cast itself as a God-fearing nation, added "Under God" to the pledge in 1954, and more public schools began reading scripture or praying before class. In 1951 the New York State Board of Regents asked religious leaders to co-write a short, non-denominational prayer, with each district deciding whether to adopt it. Districts that used the prayer let students opt out, but the parents of 10 students still sued. In 1962 Engel v. Vitale held it unconstitutional 6 to 1; the key was not whether it was compulsory but that the prayer was written by the government, which itself constituted an establishment of religion. Justice Black quoted Madison: it is proper to take alarm at the first experiment on our liberties; the same authority that could establish Christianity to the exclusion of other religions could easily establish one Christian sect. The ruling provoked fierce backlash, and the plaintiff families were mocked and harassed.

18:31 An armband is constitutional expression
In December 1965, middle and high school students in Des Moines planned to wear black armbands to class to protest American involvement in the Vietnam War. School officials announced in advance that refusal to remove them would mean suspension, and some students — including four siblings — wore the armbands anyway and were suspended. In 1969 the Supreme Court ruled for the students 7 to 2. The issue was that this was not ordinary dress or grooming but quiet, passive expression close to pure speech, and it did not disrupt class. Absent evidence of actual or provably imminent substantial interference with instruction, school officials may not suppress student opinion. The ruling said: public schools may not become totalitarian enclaves, and students and teachers do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate. This "substantial disruption" standard later became the baseline for free speech on campus. Justice Black dissented that students would from then on resist almost every school rule, and the host says on the show that this slippery-slope argument sounds rather absurd.

24:40 A school-funded newspaper can be censored
In 1983 two pieces in the Hazelwood East High School student newspaper The Spectrum troubled principal Reynolds: a story on teen pregnancy that used pseudonyms but might still make the interviewees identifiable, and a divorce story that named and criticised a student's parent. Reynolds decided to cut both entire pages rather than just remove the articles, on the grounds that there was no time to revise and the paper had to come out before the semester ended. In 1988 the Supreme Court ruled for the school 5 to 3. The key distinction is between tolerating student speech and promoting it: this newspaper was funded and published by the school, readers would take its contents as endorsed by the school, and the two pieces were indeed ethically immature as journalism. The Court held that the school has the right to control what it promotes. The rights established in Tinker were thereby given their first clear boundary.

29:46 Corporal punishment is not an Eighth Amendment matter
Host Tracy suddenly recalls that many teachers kept wooden paddles on their desks when she was a child, and on looking it up finds corporal punishment has still not died out in the United States. In the 1977 case Ingram v. Wright, the school's rule specified a paddle under two feet long, three or four inches wide and half an inch thick, in principle one to five swats; but Ingram was struck more than 20 times in a single incident and needed medical attention. The Supreme Court did not dwell on whether that instance was excessive, but held that school corporal punishment does not violate the Constitution. The reasoning: the Eighth Amendment protects those who have been convicted, and prisoners are separated from schoolchildren by the harsh facts of criminal conviction and imprisonment; schools are open places, with teachers and classmates as witnesses, and you can go home after school. According to NEA figures, corporal punishment remains legal in public schools in 17 states and is actually practised in 14, with boys, Black students and students with disabilities struck at significantly higher rates.

33:52 A bag search needs only reasonable suspicion
In 1980 in New Jersey, a 14-year-old student known as TLO was reported by a teacher for smoking in the restroom. Vice principal Choplik searched her purse, saw cigarettes and rolling papers, kept looking, and found what appeared to be marijuana and evidence of drug dealing; TLO was ultimately convicted and given a year's probation. In 1985 the Supreme Court upheld the search 6 to 3. The ruling acknowledged that the Fourth Amendment binds school officials and that students have a privacy expectation, but that this must be balanced against the school's need to maintain a learning environment. So school searches need not meet the probable cause police require; the lower threshold of reasonable suspicion suffices. The teacher's report that TLO was smoking gave the vice principal reason to suspect she had cigarettes, and a purse is exactly where they would be; seeing rolling papers naturally extended the suspicion to marijuana, which was equally reasonable.

item.title: To Make Criticism Land, Lead With High Standards and Trust
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-thinkfast-批评想被听进去-先给高期待与信任/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-thinkfast-批评想被听进去-先给高期待与信任/
item.description: Getting criticism believed isn't about opening with a few compliments — it's about showing the other person that the bar is high and that you believe they can reach it. In one experiment, a single line — "the standard is high, but you can meet it" — pushed Black students' rate of revising their essays to the highest of any condition.
item.content:encoded:
Getting criticism believed isn't about opening with a few compliments — it's about showing the other person that the bar is high and that you believe they can reach it. In one experiment, a single line — "the standard is high, but you can meet it" — pushed Black students' rate of revising their essays to the highest of any condition.

The person who proposed stereotype threat research breaks down the mechanism herself and grounds the intervention in a replicable experimental script. Twenty minutes of high information density, with none of the vague communication chicken soup.

1:04 Identity bias makes people underperform on the spot
When a situation carries a negative label about one of your identities, and that situation matters to you, you worry about being judged by that label. This worry comes from the situation itself: it depresses performance on tests, sports or intellectual tasks in the moment, and it also makes people avoid such situations over the long run, which in turn shapes who they befriend, where they live, and which schools they send their kids to. The anxiety doesn't come from ability; it comes from the expectation of being defined by the label.

3:10 Social media lets labels chase you down
Social media's power lies in how fast it spreads sketches of what a group is like. People have no patience to see the full picture and the exceptions, so it naturally multiplies the number of situations in which you might be seen through your identity. Occasionally it also spreads images that reduce threat, but the overall tone skews negative, and the result is that in a diverse society, everyone is more on guard about their identity and about what others might be thinking.

6:16 A 15-minute self-affirmation exercise lifts grades
In racially integrated classrooms, Black students live with the constant possibility that their ability is being underestimated. Teachers simply asked seventh graders to spend 15 minutes writing a short essay about the people and things they valued most. White students were barely affected, but Black students used the occasion to let the teacher know "I'm not just that label," and their grades began to rise, setting off a positive feedback loop: better grades → less vigilance about the label → still better grades. The intervention cost almost nothing, yet it changed long-term trajectories.

9:20 Vigilance in diverse settings: remember or forget
The author calls this state churn. In settings where people of different backgrounds are together and the outcome matters, people are pulled back and forth between two choices: remember that "others might read me through my group's stereotype" to protect themselves, or simply forget it, relax, and trust the person in front of them. This isn't fragility; it's the real pressure the situation creates, and when the setting matters, it continuously drains attention that should be going to the task.

12:24 High standards plus trust make feedback work
In an experiment, students wrote an essay about their favorite teacher and received critical feedback. Under the first two approaches — giving it straight, or opening with a "positive hat" — white students trusted the feedback, while Black students were highly distrustful. The third approach added just one line: "We have high standards, because these essays will be published; I read your essay and I believe you can meet them." Under that condition, Black students took their essays home to revise at three times the rate of the other conditions.

14:26 You can't assume others already trust you
After years as a dean and provost, Claude believes the most useful skill is realizing that everyone you work with needs that signal of respect. Society's common mistake is assuming trust already exists, when in reality people worry about how you see the group they belong to. Truly effective leaders are good at giving that signal first: even if an employee disagrees with a decision, as long as they feel the other person respects who they are and their potential, the team atmosphere is completely different.

17:35 Let people see you're human before you talk trust
Claude breaks good communication into three things: first, let the other person know you understand what this situation means to them — when power is unequal, the person with more power has to send the safety signal first; second, near-obsessive clarity, because beating around the bush destroys valuable information; third, warmth and goodwill, because people need to confirm that the person across from them is a good person before they hand over trust. Matt sums it up as connect, be clear, care.

item.title: Latin Doesn't Make Surgeons: A Hard Exam Is Worth Less Than a Useful One
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-econtalk-拉丁文练不出外科医生-考试难-不如考得有用/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-econtalk-拉丁文练不出外科医生-考试难-不如考得有用/
item.description: Latin doesn't make surgeons: skills barely transfer. If you assume harder material sharpens the mind, a nation's brightest get wasted on its most useless knowledge — that is the lesson of the Qing examination system.
item.content:encoded:
Latin doesn't make surgeons: skills barely transfer. If you assume harder material sharpens the mind, a nation's brightest get wasted on its most useless knowledge — that is the lesson of the Qing examination system.

It puts imperial civil-service exams, military selection and modern transfer experiments on a single chain of evidence, unusually connecting history with talent assessment — and the two sides genuinely clash.

10:03 Wrong exam content dooms the country, however smart the candidates
Hong Xiuquan failed the Qing examinations at least four times. After the last failure, on the road home, he had a vision, believed himself the brother of Christ, and eventually launched the Taiping Rebellion — which Daisy says may be the deadliest civil war in human history, with deaths perhaps around thirty million. He was not alone: examination seats fell far short of the number of candidates, many sat until their forties or fifties without passing, and the only way home was to teach. Daisy adds that the deeper cost fell on those who did pass: they were masters of the eight-legged essay yet knew nothing of the science and mathematics then changing the world. When the brightest young men can only drill a dead format, the country bleeds from both ends.

22:51 British civil-service reform was elites reproducing themselves
The Northcote-Trevelyan report is often seen by the British as the founding document of the modern civil service, but Daisy backs the revisionist reading: in the name of a unified exam, it pushed Oxford and Cambridge classics graduates into key posts. Benjamin Jowett, master of Balliol, worked behind the scenes to place his classics students throughout the empire. Michael Coolican's "No Tradesmen and No Women" points out that the 1854 report reduced the crudest buying and selling of offices, but also snuffed out the professional exams then growing inside individual departments. Exams can select people; what they examine decides whether they select the able or select people like themselves.

35:58 A bureaucracy with no price signal corrects itself through corpses
Daisy attributes bureaucratic failure to the absence of feedback: no price mechanism, no profit and loss, so a department cannot tell whether its program saves or kills. The military sounds like a counterexample, but military bureaucracies err just as constantly in peacetime; almost every time Britain went to war after a long peace, a crisis brewed in the first year, as with the shell crisis at the start of World War I. What actually forces correction is not internal inspection but mass death on the battlefield. She calls it a crueler error-correction mechanism than prices. To make a bureaucracy reliable you first need a signal that shows consequences; otherwise no severity of selection can rescue the quality of everyday decisions.

43:06 The Royal Navy won by examining navigation, not Latin
Daisy notes that Britain's real pillar in the Victorian era was not the army but the Royal Navy. As early as 1677, after a run of defeats by the Dutch, Samuel Pepys set an oral exam for captains: three senior officers questioned them face to face on how to command a ship. Over the next century and more, navigation, charting and trigonometry entered the written exams, and chart-makers like Nelson, Cook, Flinders and Bligh passed through that gate. Daisy draws out two exam traditions: Pepys tested skills needed immediately; Macaulay and Northcote-Trevelyan later wanted classical languages tested. One served safety at sea, the other a layer of status, and the results differed accordingly.

47:31 Content doesn't matter? Macaulay's screening argument misses one thing
Here comes the highlight: Daisy reads Macaulay's 1833 parliamentary speech aloud. The gist: whatever a age happens to teach, those who excel at it will be the cleverest, most industrious and most honor-seeking of the young; so Cambridge could teach Ptolemy instead of Newton and its top students would still be excellent; teach Cherokee instead of Greek and the best Cherokee scholars would still be the best men; even astrology and alchemy would do. Another MP called it on the spot the most practical-wisdom speech in parliamentary history, but Daisy says flatly: this is a man carried away by his own eloquence, missing entirely that what you learn really does matter.

51:21 Dead twigs and corn: wrong content makes discipline just watering
Daisy closes on Macaulay with the 1917 rebuttal of the American medical educator Abraham Flexner. Flexner said the devotees of mental training resemble Egyptian priests: they stick a row of dead twigs in the soil and then water them faithfully for the sake of discipline. Plant corn and the discipline is no less, with a crop thrown in. Against the American medical schools of the day, where many aspiring doctors were forced through Greek and Latin before touching a medical book, Flexner's answer was: medicine is already hard enough, and using it to sharpen the mind is far more efficient than using dead languages. Daisy agrees: spend the best years of the most gifted on what has been disproved or is useless, and the winners will be rivals who let their young learn real knowledge.

59:21 Rectangles don't train triangles: transfer needs identical elements
Thorndike designed a cleaner controlled experiment: have people repeatedly estimate the area of rectangles until they clearly improve, then have them estimate the area of triangles — almost no transfer. If even two shapes this close show nothing, the claim that classical languages sharpen the mind is even less credible. Thorndike's explanation was identical elements: transfer appears only when old and new tasks share the same components; far transfer essentially breaks down. Daisy draws the exam-design principle from this: to select people who can navigate, examine navigation and trigonometry; to select people who can practice medicine, examine medicine. An exam that actually works wires its difficulty straight into the real task.

item.title: Global liquidity peaks: the companies that spent most aggressively on AI in H1 are discounted first
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-cn38ff4a-全球流动性见顶-上半年越激进砸-ai-的公司-越先被折价/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-cn38ff4a-全球流动性见顶-上半年越激进砸-ai-的公司-越先被折价/
item.description: A rising market needs new money to keep taking the other side. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that invested most aggressively in AI in the first half are turning from rewarded to discounted.
item.content:encoded:
A rising market needs new money to keep taking the other side. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that invested most aggressively in AI in the first half are turning from rewarded to discounted.

It puts US AI capex, Hong Kong IPOs and household balance sheets on the same funding chain — a macro framework that does not treat AI as a panacea.

0:33 A low IPO break rate is not a good signal
Do not read Hong Kong's low first-day break rate as a strengthening market. In the first half of this year the break rate was only in the teens, far below the roughly fifty-fifty level normal under a market-based mechanism — meaning the money subscribing to new listings is mostly short-term speculative arbitrage, not long-term investors. Recently the supply of new listings has shrunk and a subscription-related fund blew up, yet the two most recent listings still broke issue, showing that temporary control on the supply side has not fixed the underlying problem: Hong Kong faces the same peaking liquidity.

12:07 The more aggressive on AI, the sooner you are punished
Market attitude reversed within a single quarter. Before Q1, the capital market rewarded aggression: the louder the AI CapEx, the higher the valuation. By the time half-year reports were disclosed in late July, any large internet company that had made aggressive capex in the first half — especially one that spent its free cash flow to zero — was discounted, and even Google was not exempt. Q2 was precisely the quarter of maximum FOMO across the whole supply chain, with everyone rushing to spend before prices rose and inventory still able to hold up gross margin; by Q3, when inventory is exhausted and the price increases come back, the negatives will show up together.

15:54 Nvidia is closer to Cisco in 2000
Nvidia's earnings look good, but its cash flow is changing shape. Before the internet bubble burst in 2000, Cisco rolled out rent-to-buy to help customers finance purchases, pulling future revenue forward into reported sales; Nvidia is now pushing rent-to-buy as well. Free cash flow in the report halved quarter on quarter, and receivables on the books are far above historical levels — speculated to be partly tied to the credit enhancement and collection structure that rent-to-buy brings. Nvidia may therefore have reached the stage where it needs more aggressive financial engineering to sustain capital-market expectations, which resembles Cisco's position back then.

33:21 Primary-market money is bullets from three years ago
The answer lies in when the funds raised. The money being deployed into AI and robotics from H2 2025 through H1 2026 mainly comes from funds raised at the 2020-2022 market peak; from 2023 to 2025 they barely invested, until they saw state capital placing bets in a period when no one dared to and earning the most — the stories of ChangXin and ChangCun, the two large model companies and the two large chip companies stirred market-based capital, and the mindset became: copy the state capital's homework. So this is not a rational long-term increment; it looks more like a delayed emotional release.

47:31 The property policy detaches households from the funding chain
The key to recent real estate policy is not bailing out developers but pulling households out of the old financing loop. Buying a pre-sale home used to mean the household played the role of financing counterparty in the investment-driven chain: pay first, receive the home later; by pushing the chain toward a market-based model, the policy means buyers get completed homes and bear only the consumer role, with risk reset back onto developers and financing institutions. The policy was timed for when prices were near the bottom in order to first stabilise the denominator on the asset side, avoiding panic from dismantling the chain during a decline. Japan after the 1990s and the consolidation of China's coal and mining industries both went down similar paths.

1:01:34 A slow bull is not a slogan, it is a chip structure
A slow bull does not come from shouting; it comes from layering market chips by duration: at the bottom, low-valuation high-dividend blue chips taken up by insurers as long money that rarely trades; above that, mutual funds and index funds performing a quasi-stabilisation function; above that, China Securities Finance and Central Huijin adjusting the index; and only at the top, retail, private funds and active managers. The new insurance rules require liabilities and assets to match on duration, yield and liquidity — institutionally ensuring long money invests long, medium money medium, short money short: you are not allowed to take ordinary people's short money and put it into ten-year illiquid assets.

1:22:49 Crises get bigger with each rescue, and bubbles at least one and a half times
After the dollar left gold in 1971, global central banks became increasingly used to intervening in crises directly by printing money, each time faster than the last. The quantitative easing after 2008 should have been cleared out during the rate-hiking cycle, but political intervention cut it short, and then came the pandemic in 2020, so on top of a bubble that had not yet dissipated another, larger wave of easing was layered — at least one and a half bubbles accumulated by today. Central bank governors have learned to print more money the moment a crisis appears, and the endogenous result is inflation, rising financial assets and widening wealth inequality all at once. As long as the bubble is not allowed to clear, the world may face a form of long-term stagflation.

item.title: Central Banks Won't Kill the $100 Bill: It's a $2.5 Trillion Interest-Free Loan
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-oddlots-央行不愿废除百元美钞-那是一笔-2-5-万亿无息贷款/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-oddlots-央行不愿废除百元美钞-那是一笔-2-5-万亿无息贷款/
item.description: Cash use keeps falling, yet currency in circulation keeps hitting records. Central banks have an incentive to keep printing $100 bills: the money is effectively a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the U.S. government, and the price is convenience for money launderers worldwide.
item.content:encoded:
Cash use keeps falling, yet currency in circulation keeps hitting records. Central banks have an incentive to keep printing $100 bills: the money is effectively a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the U.S. government, and the price is convenience for money launderers worldwide.

It strips money laundering back from "bank wires" to watches, tractors, casino chips and VAT loopholes, and explains why central banks can't bear to kill the $100 bill.

5:09 The scale of money laundering hasn't changed in thirty years
The most commonly used estimate of money laundering is 2% to 5% of global GDP per year, which at today's roughly $100 trillion GDP is $2 trillion to $5 trillion. That figure comes from a rough estimate by former IMF managing director Michel Camdessus in the late 1990s, and no one has come up with a better answer since. Oliver warns that the more alarming fact is that this ratio hasn't changed in thirty years: decades of anti-money-laundering action have not shrunk the criminal economy, only barely held it back from growing faster than the overall economy.

9:10 Banks spend $200 billion a year on AML for near-zero effect
When banks complain that KYC is too expensive, it isn't just whining. The U.S. passed the Bank Secrecy Act in 1970, and in 1989 the FATF turned anti-money-laundering into a global norm, forcing banks to hire compliance teams and install AI monitoring software. LexisNexis estimates global AML compliance costs about $200 billion a year, enough to solve world hunger and provide clean water to everyone. Yet the system generates enormous numbers of suspicious activity reports every year, and launderers still run ahead of regulators. The problem isn't that banks aren't trying; it's that the whole system is expensive, weakly feedback-driven, and almost no one is accountable for outcomes.

12:14 Trade-based laundering is an order of magnitude bigger than cash smuggling
Cash smuggling makes money laundering inside the banking system look small by comparison, but the bigger chunk never touches money at all: value is hidden in goods. Mexico takes in about $25 billion in cash a year, while John Deere and Caterpillar farm equipment exported from the U.S. becomes the consideration cartels get back; European luxury goods flow to China, and drugs and goods are imported back in the China direction, with the triangle settled through misinvoicing. Global Financial Integrity estimates this kind of trade-based laundering at about $1 trillion a year. A million-dollar watch on your wrist through customs is far easier than moving a million in cash.

17:18 The Vancouver model: Chinese cash demand meets cartel supply
Each person in China has only a $50,000 annual foreign-exchange quota, while wealthy Chinese have plenty of demand to spend abroad. The Vancouver model matches that demand with the dollar cash supply from drug cartels: bags of cash outside Canadian casinos are handed to Chinese gamblers, the money is lost at the tables, and the gamblers run up gambling debts; that debt is offset on the other end in China by an RMB transaction and the drug sales that follow. Looked at as just the gambling round, it looks like a loss; looked at across the whole chain, it is a triangular settlement that simultaneously repatriates cartel money and moves Chinese capital out. The model later spread worldwide, with luxury goods, consumer goods and drugs all serving as vehicles for moving value.

23:25 A VAT loophole lets the same goods extract 20% over and over
Zero-rated cross-border transactions in the EU were meant to keep national tax authorities from having to audit each other, but they became an ATM: goods entering the UK from Ireland don't owe VAT, and when sold to an affiliated shell company 20% is added; that shell company then re-exports the goods back to Ireland and can claim a refund from the UK tax authority of the 20% that was never paid. Round and round it goes, hence carousel fraud. The UK once largely suppressed it with a multi-agency crackdown, and the fraudsters then moved to continental Europe, where it now runs about €50 billion a year, spreading from Lithuania all the way to Portugal. Criminal organizations have no ceiling on cooperation: the more they cooperate, the bigger they get.

27:27 Nobody uses cash, yet central banks are printing record notes
In the digital-payments era, cash transactions are down to about 9% in the UK and about 13% in the U.S., so by ordinary logic the supply of paper money should be shrinking. After Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey raised the banknote paradox in 2009, the phenomenon only intensified: the value of UK notes in circulation doubled, and the U.S. is approaching $2.5 trillion. Central banks blaming it on "store of value" doesn't hold up — surveys show the average American adult has only a bit over $400 on them, while per-capita U.S. currency in circulation works out to more than $7,000. The Fed estimates about 65% of U.S. bills are abroad, but that only pushes the question past the border: no one knows whose hands these notes are actually sitting in.

32:31 The $100 bill is a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the government
Seigniorage can't simply be understood as the profit from printing money: a $100 bill costs 9 cents, but it isn't "sold" to you — you can always exchange it back for goods at face value, so the cash the public holds is essentially an interest-free loan. With close to $2.5 trillion of U.S. currency in circulation, the U.S. government gets interest-free funding equal to about 6% of the national debt; federal interest payments are now about 19% of the budget, and if that $2.5 trillion also had to pay interest, you'd add roughly another percentage point. This is exactly why central banks don't want to hear anyone discuss abolishing cash.

47:51 AML incentives are inverted: the more reports, the less crime gets policed
Suspicious activity reports were supposed to be real-time intelligence for law enforcement, but reality is the exact opposite: banks hire thousands of compliance officers to fill out reports, law enforcement has no resources to read them, and most reports fall into a black hole; a bank that fails to file can be fined in the billions, while doing it right earns no reward. The side effects include debanking — large numbers of people who are merely suspected, many of them Muslim, get cut off from financial institutions. The guest's solution isn't to hire more compliance officers but to generate fewer reports, actually read them, and genuinely prosecute financial criminals, raising the cost of money laundering instead of drowning everyone in paperwork.

item.title: Russia Is Stuck in Ukraine, but Still Has Room to Open a New Front Against NATO
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-hiddenforces-俄罗斯陷在乌克兰-仍有余力对北约开新战线/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-hiddenforces-俄罗斯陷在乌克兰-仍有余力对北约开新战线/
item.description: Russia has not won in Ukraine, but its war of attrition has forged the world's most advanced drone-infantry combat experience; the guest argues it has ample capacity to mount a limited probe against NATO, and the window is in the final phase of Trump's term.
item.content:encoded:
Russia has not won in Ukraine, but its war of attrition has forged the world's most advanced drone-infantry combat experience; the guest argues it has ample capacity to mount a limited probe against NATO, and the window is in the final phase of Trump's term.

The guest is the Wall Street Journal's chief diplomatic correspondent, and was in Kyiv on the day of the 2022 invasion; his judgments on Russian military capability and Europe's fractures are far more concrete than those of TV commentators.

19:16 Trump's anti-Europe talk may be taken literally by Putin
Everyone is speculating about whether John Ratcliffe's secret trip to Russia was there to negotiate terms. The guest's judgment is that the visit looks more like carrying a message to Moscow on Trump's behalf: don't take those on-air remarks about ‘America not caring about Europe’ seriously — if Russia invades Lithuania, Estonia or Finland, the US will send troops. The reasoning is that Moscow is bogged down in a war of attrition in Ukraine and badly needs to cut off European support for Ukraine, so escalating with a probe against NATO is one option, while Trump's earlier statements that ‘Europe is a bunch of freeloaders’ gave Putin room to misread, hence the need for a dedicated trip to make the red line clear. One caveat: the guest does not have intelligence from inside that room; he is explaining why the account ‘makes complete sense’, not confirming it.

21:27 Russia's army isn't exhausted — it can still open a limited front
Russia has been unable to take Ukraine for a long time — does that mean it cannot open another front? The guest's answer is blunt: it can absolutely open a ‘limited front’ — not tanks rolling across Poland to Paris, but something in the Baltic direction, such as blockading the narrow land corridor of the Suwalki Gap. He says the Russian and Ukrainian armies are the only two in the world today that fight modern drone-infantry warfare as a daily routine. The story of a 20-man Ukrainian drone team destroying an entire traditional battalion is widely told, but the Russian military has the same technology in hand: 20 Russians can likewise wipe out a NATO battalion that has had no anti-drone training. Outsiders assume Russia grows weaker the longer it fights, but overlook that it is also one of the parties being tempered by this technological revolution.

22:31 NATO might not even rescue Lithuania from Poland
A war game designed to simulate a Russian invasion of Lithuania led the guest to a deeply unsettling conclusion: even Poland did not send troops to save Lithuania, let alone other allies. The reason is not insufficient military power, but that Russian forces advance too fast and nuclear deterrence hangs over everything, so allies fall into hesitation over ‘whether to enter’, producing a chain of waiting and watching. The guest says Moscow has factored exactly this into its options. He also cautions that this is not quite the same as before 2022 — back then, a hundred thousand-plus Russian troops massing could be clearly seen on the German and Belarusian borders, and there is no such material preparation now. So the most immediate escalation may not be a conventional invasion, but small, ambiguous attacks that can be denied (hitting a warehouse or a drone first).

23:40 Russia is already probing NATO's limits with drones
At this stage, with no sign of a massed army on the border, Russia still holds a set of low-cost, low-attribution options: a limited strike on a NATO warehouse near Poland or Romania, or a provocation using a captured Ukrainian drone that has been modified, then watching whether NATO splits and whether the US steps in. The guest notes this kind of probing is already underway — an armed drone attacked a Ukrainian aircraft parked at Leipzig airport in Germany, and only a drone malfunction prevented casualties; Russian risk-taking is rising steadily, and the West has so far given no serious response. The senior European officers he has spoken with all believe the most dangerous window is the next one to two years, roughly falling in the final phase of Trump's term — the Kremlin will want to act before the US might let go.

27:53 Putin wants Ukraine disarmed, not a ceasefire
Would Putin accept a decent ceasefire deal? The guest's view is that you only have to look at what is put on the table: Russia has consistently demanded not just territory, but a cap on the size of Ukraine's army, limits on the types of weapons it may hold, and a cutoff of Western military aid to Ukraine. In his words, the goal is to make Ukraine ‘lose the ability to defend itself’; not neutral, but ‘castrated’, so that it cannot rise again in the next phase of the war — a year, five years or ten years later. Putin signed Minsk-1 and Minsk-2, and violated both. So the guest quotes the summary of Ukraine's former foreign minister: this war can only end one of two ways — the end of Ukraine, or the end of the Russian imperial project. Waiting for the other side to change its mind is not on the menu.

31:08 Street protests can decide who stays in the wartime cabinet
Kyiv's recent personnel earthquake looks on the surface like an anti-corruption storm, but the key mechanism lies elsewhere: elections are frozen in wartime, and the president's legitimacy rests on just one ballast stone — ‘street support’. Zelensky initially fired Defense Minister Fedorov, who had pushed drone innovation, because he needed the backing of Commander-in-Chief Syrsky; after Fedorov was dismissed, Kyiv's elites took to the streets, and the protests, small as they were, were enough to make the president reverse course — he removed Syrsky, brought in a younger general more popular with the front line, and appointed a defense minister with a veteran intelligence background acceptable to all sides. Ukraine's independent anti-corruption bodies can still pursue people in the president's innermost circle, and when Zelensky tried to amend the law to absorb that body, he backed down within a week under street pressure. When elections are absent, the square equals the ballot box.

38:37 Resistance comes from memory, not heroism
Summing up Ukrainian perseverance as patriotic heroism misses what actually drives them. The guest says that after Russian troops take a Ukrainian town, one of the first things they often do is send bulldozers to tear down monuments to the victims of the 1930s famine — what they want to delete is a memory. Russian state television talks about how to ‘re-educate’ Ukrainians, making them forget their language and culture and become Russians. Around World War II, the Soviet Union carried out a systematic purge of Ukraine's cultural elite, and in the guest's childhood he had no idea those writers existed, because collective memory had been erased. Ukrainians today are almost all descendants of survivors of that meat grinder of history, carrying the trauma in their bodies; it is precisely the fear of ‘never again’ that makes them prefer to die on the battlefield rather than return to that life.

45:59 Half a million veterans blocked the first wave of collapse
On the night of February 23, 2022, most people in Kyiv still did not believe there would be a war; the guest remembers knowing from his experience in Kabul and Baghdad that ‘impossible’ can flip overnight, but ordinary Ukrainians had no such reference point. What really kept the country from collapsing in the first days was eight years of war in the Donbas: that fighting was far from Kyiv, but it produced roughly 500,000 Ukrainians who had traded blows with the Russian army, and volunteer organizations that evolved into a flexible, aggressive force. The psychological threshold had already been crossed in the Donbas — ‘we know what they look like, we know how to fight them’. Because of that experience, the swift collapse Putin expected did not happen, and the West's widespread expectations were wrong too.

item.title: A Preschooler Hitting, Biting or Kicking Isn't Bad Behavior — It's a Fight to Get the Body Back
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-parentmojo-孩子打咬踢不是坏行为-是在夺回身体自主权/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-parentmojo-孩子打咬踢不是坏行为-是在夺回身体自主权/
item.description: Stop asking how to make the hitting stop. For a three- or four-year-old, hitting, biting and kicking are often the only tool left to shout "I have no say" after adults have taken control of nearly everything — give back a little choice and the behavior shrinks.
item.content:encoded:
Stop asking how to make the hitting stop. For a three- or four-year-old, hitting, biting and kicking are often the only tool left to shout "I have no say" after adults have taken control of nearly everything — give back a little choice and the behavior shrinks.

Most approaches restate "no hitting" and add punishment, never touching the need that comes before the behavior. This episode treats aggression as a need signal, and models the scripts and cases for negotiating with teachers.

4:21 A child who hits is shouting that he has no say over his body
Preschool is often the first place a child is controlled in nearly every bodily arrangement by an adult other than his parents: where to sit, how to sit, when to speak and when to move. For the previous three years he could roughly decide when to run and when to use the toilet. Sitting on a rug for 20 minutes without moving is a real deprivation of autonomy; and a three- or four-year-old has no language to assert "my body is mine to decide," so hitting and kicking become one of the few tools still available. So when the call home comes, don't rush to lecture "hands to yourself." Ask instead: how much say did this child have over his own life before this, and what little bit of it can be handed back now.

6:42 Kindergarten readiness is, in substance, obedience training
Teachers often say a given preschool has a high share of kindergarten-ready children, and the core definition of that readiness is compliance: sit down when the teacher says sit, even mid-task, even when the body is already overloaded. Parents fear that if the child doesn't comply now, he won't get into a good elementary school, college, a good life. But the price the child pays for that definition is learning to suppress the feeling of "what I need right now." Teachers aren't villains either — they too need to feel competent, to keep children safe, to save effort, and even to enjoy a taste of power; many went into education precisely to repair their own childhood wounds, yet only know the power-over kind of relationship. Only by seeing both sides' situations is there room to negotiate.

9:24 We grant ourselves regulation and deny it to children
If an adult at a party feels overloaded, he arrives early, leaves early, hides in a quiet room, even wears noise-cancelling earplugs — we find that entirely natural. Turn the camera on a child, though, and apart from routines like extra exam time, we immediately worry that "too much accommodation will spoil him, he'll never survive the real world." The truth is that adults grant themselves far more accommodation than they allow children. The source offers a concrete image: an adult stronger than you unceremoniously carries you out of the quiet room back into the middle of the loud party — as an adult you'd instantly see that as a violation of bodily autonomy; when it happens to a child we look right past it.

12:11 The repair point is before the behavior, not the behavior itself
Repeating "hitting is not okay" doesn't work, because that isn't knowledge the child is missing. You need a different set of questions: what happened in the few seconds before this bite? What happened earlier in the day? Is there a move or a new baby in the child's life right now? A sensory-overloaded child who gets jostled in line will melt down, so let him stand at the front, the back, or outside the line; a child who struggles with transitions needs a few minutes' warning. An adult analogy: when your partner snaps at you for no reason at night, it's usually not about that sentence but about the morning's argument, lost sleep and a pile of stress. If the other person then tossed off "your attitude needs some work," you'd blow up too — yet we routinely do only the latter to children.

15:10 Talking to the teacher: don't assign blame, hear what the "no" is protecting
Telling a teacher "please change what you're doing" will almost certainly hit a wall. A safer opening is to drop judgment and reconstruct the facts: not who's responsible, just what actually happened; and include family changes, which are context the teacher can't see. Once you know whether the child's trigger is sensory or autonomy, extend empathy to the three things behind the teacher: competence, the child's safety, and the effort saved by a breather. The request must land on a concrete, doable change, like "can he sit on a ball outside the circle." If the teacher refuses, the key word isn't refusal but what need that "no" is still protecting, and finding a different arrangement that satisfies both sides.

16:07 One nap-time conflict, cleanly taken apart
Jen's daughter Carys, at three, couldn't nap, and the teacher wanted her to lie down; she was bored and frustrated — her need was to play. The teacher had two needs: state rules required offering a nap, and nap time was the teacher's own break. The solution they found was to move her mat to a slightly separated corner, where she could quietly play with soft toys that wouldn't roll, and the teacher could see her through the window from the break room. The child kept her right to free play, the teacher kept the rule and the rest, and Jen escaped the no-win cycle of incident reports. This segment shows that "negotiating by need" isn't empty talk: everyone gives a little, but everyone's core need is held.

17:53 Every method comes down to one question in the end
Compress all of the above into one line: stop asking "how do I make the hitting stop," and ask "what need is this behavior communicating?" Hitting, biting and kicking are only surface signals; the real message may be "I need sensory relief" or "I need some say over my own body." Once the need is correctly named, a path to meeting it can be designed; and it is almost always the adult who changes the environment, because changing how the adult shows up is far easier than changing the child.

item.title: The Thai Flood That Wrecked the Hard Disk Drive Industry: The Biggest Factory Fell, the Number Two Took the Throne
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-asianometry-泰国洪水重创硬盘业-最大的厂跌倒-老二捡了王座/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-asianometry-泰国洪水重创硬盘业-最大的厂跌倒-老二捡了王座/
item.description: One flood in Thailand redrew the hard drive rankings: the largest maker, Western Digital, saw shipments fall 51% quarter over quarter, while Seagate fell only 8% and overtook it to take the top spot.
item.content:encoded:
One flood in Thailand redrew the hard drive rankings: the largest maker, Western Digital, saw shipments fall 51% quarter over quarter, while Seagate fell only 8% and overtook it to take the top spot.

This flood is a complete case study in the risks of geographically concentrated manufacturing supply chains — industrial estate siting, zero inventory and single points of failure all detonating at once.

6:13 Flood walls gave the hard drive makers a false sense of security
The industrial estates were built on river floodplain converted from rice paddies north of Bangkok. For flood protection, developers installed ring levees up to two meters high, secondary wave walls, pumps and drainage systems; the parks quickly grew into small cities with their own housing and shops. But this engineering may have misled everyone. When the real flood season arrived in 2011, seven industrial parks were inundated within two weeks. Research later suspected that it was precisely this seemingly complete infrastructure that created a kind of false confidence — the belief that even if it rained, everything would be fine. In other words, what the manufacturers bought was not safety, but an illusion about risk.

8:24 Reservoir releases were not the culprit; local rainfall was
After the flood, dam managers were blamed for releasing water too late, with criticism centering on favoritism toward farmers and rice corruption allegations. But the research does not support this attribution. A 2023 simulation ran 17 scenarios swapping the release strategies of two dams, and concluded that even with perfect foresight of subsequent rainfall, the flooded area could have been reduced by at most only 3.68%. Another 2020 study examined hydrological station data across the Chao Phraya River and found that in one low-lying disaster area, less than 30% of the floodwater came from the river, while 73.7% came from local rainfall. In other words, the water mainly fell directly on the disaster area's head, and reservoir decisions cannot carry the blame.

9:25 Why Seagate, which was not flooded, also shut down
Seagate's factories in the north at Korat were basically fine, but production still stopped — because seven of its top ten suppliers were underwater. The typical case was Japan's Nidec, which makes spindle motors for hard drives and halted production outright after two plants flooded. The hard drive supply chain interlocks layer by layer: no matter how safe the assembly line, if the motors do not arrive, the whole line stops. Seagate held its quarterly shipment decline to 8% by quickly qualifying new suppliers, modifying designs to reduce complexity, and negotiating payment terms with suppliers. In the same year, Western Digital's core plant took on water 1.8 meters deep, and its quarterly shipments fell 51%. The difference between the two was not whose building was taller, but whose supply chain underneath could route around the break point faster.

12:34 Zero inventory amplified the flood into a global shortage
Before the flood hit, the hard drive industry had just completed a round of consolidation: Western Digital announced in March 2011 that it would acquire Hitachi's hard drive business, and a month later Seagate announced it would acquire Samsung, barely bringing supply and demand back into balance. Precisely because there was no surplus inventory to draw down, the shock was multiplied. Tom Coughlin estimated that in the fourth quarter of 2011, hard drive demand was about 180 million units while actual production was only 110 million to 120 million; and the flood happened to hit right in the Christmas shopping season. Retail immediately raised spot prices by 20% to 40%, and a 1TB hard drive at Taipei's Guanghua Market went from NT$1,750 to over NT$3,000. Even Intel admitted in December that Q4 revenue would be about $1 billion less than expected because of the hard drive shortage. A localized flood, transmitted through zero inventory, thus became a global shortage.

15:41 The water receded, but hard drive prices did not fall for two years
The water receded, but the shortage did not end quickly. Hard drive supply availability only returned to pre-disaster levels about nine months later; retail prices fell back even more slowly — hard drive prices on Newegg did not drop back to pre-disaster levels until April 2013. Backblaze did the math using its own purchasing records: in September 2011 the cost per GB was $0.044, and it would take until September 2013 to return to that level again. Why is it easy to raise prices but hard to lower them? The author lists several interpretations: the ecosystem recovered more slowly than expected, the two giants' 2011 acquisitions brought extra costs, tablets caused PC hard drive demand to permanently decline, and a more cynical guess — after Seagate and Western Digital acquired their second-tier rivals, only three major manufacturers remained in the entire industry, making prices easier to ‘stabilize’, or in his own word: cartelize. As for which one is the truth, he does not conclude.

18:47 The flooded giant chose to stay and keep building walls
Western Digital's post-disaster choice is telling: it did not retreat, it doubled down on defenses. WD and the Bang Pa-in estate owner built an 11-kilometer flood wall along the estate, and WD added a 6-meter-high inner wall around its factory; to add redundancy to its supply chain, in December 2011 it announced a new slider fab in Malaysia. A survey of 50 directly affected Japanese companies showed that nearly 80% decided to stay in Thailand. The reasons are not hard to understand: ready-made estates, supporting infrastructure and skilled workers are hard to pack up and take away. Thailand has since suffered multiple rounds of major flooding, especially in the 2020s when it happened almost every year; in November of the most recent year it even rained what was billed as a ‘once in 300 years’ rain, but these estates have held so far. Whether stronger defenses will be needed in the future can only be tested by the next major flood.

item.title: AI Designs a Virus That Infects Bacteria, but Only 5% of the Time
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-twiv-ai-设计出能感染细菌的病毒-但成功率仅-5/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-twiv-ai-设计出能感染细菌的病毒-但成功率仅-5/
item.description: For the first time, AI designed a complete viral genome that infects bacteria from scratch; experimental validation succeeded only about 5% of the time, far from the all-powerful picture the media painted.
item.content:encoded:
For the first time, AI designed a complete viral genome that infects bacteria from scratch; experimental validation succeeded only about 5% of the time, far from the all-powerful picture the media painted.

This episode takes apart the success rate of AI-made viruses, compensatory mutations and biosafety rhetoric, while demonstrating how an observational vaccine study can be falsified by an E-value.

12:43 A vaccine switch as a natural control
The trap in "healthy vaccinee bias" is that vaccinated people tend to pay more attention to their own health than unvaccinated people, so comparing the two groups mistakes lifestyle differences for vaccine effects. This study exploits the moment in 2017 when the US shingles vaccine switched wholesale from Zostavax to Shingrix: before the policy switch people received the old vaccine, after it they received the new one, and both groups were people who actively sought vaccination, so in theory the bias is erased. It is still not a randomised trial, however — socioeconomic status, smoking, diet and other unmeasured factors may still be unbalanced between the two groups, so it counts only as a quasi-experiment.

15:47 Weak confounding alone can overturn a vaccine benefit
How strong would unmeasured confounding have to be to overturn an observational conclusion? Measure it with the E-value. The E-value for this vaccine study is only 1.42, almost touching 1, meaning a confounder that is not even very strong but is associated with both "which vaccine was received" and "cardiovascular outcome" could explain away the observed risk reduction. An E-value needs to reach 3.4 or even 5 for a conclusion to count as solid; 1.42 is far from robust. The authors themselves admit that a randomised clinical trial is needed to confirm it, and that this observation cannot be treated as evidence.

38:13 AI produces a functional viral genome for the first time
The researchers took the genomic language models EVO1 and EVO2 and had them write phage genomes: first the models read massive public DNA sequence data, then they were fine-tuned on PhiX174 to generate thousands of candidate sequences. Back in the lab for validation, only about 5% of the products could actually infect E. coli — the first time AI has designed a complete genome from scratch and had it proven functional. If the media summarise this as "AI directly made a virus", they miss a key point: the model had only seen sequences, with no experimental annotation telling it which base does what, and the 5% hit rate shows how ignorant it still is about how sequence determines function.

44:37 The origin of replication is the model's most conserved memory
The only prompt the model needed was the first 4 to 9 nucleotides of the PhiX174 genome, and the accuracy of the generated results rose significantly. The authors found that this unremarkable stretch is part of the origin of replication, and it was 100% conserved across all the genomes the model generated. It is like a password saying "I am a real virus": the model treats the origin of replication as a core that must be locked down, and only dares to let other positions evolve freely. This also explains why such a short prompt works — what matters is not the prompt's length but whether it hits a functional pressure point.

56:55 AI swaps one gene and supplies 58 mutations itself
The design idea behind EVO36 was not to rewrite a whole segment but to swap genes: replace PhiX174's J gene with the shorter J protein from phage G4. When humans did the same transplant by hand in the past, the product could not infect; but the AI's EVO36 infects normally, because it accumulated 58 additional mutations across the genome. These mutations look like compensatory mutations that let the foreign J protein re-adapt to its local environment. Humans might not think to touch 58 positions at once, and this is exactly where generative models exceed the power of single-point editing.

1:00:15 Mixed phages specifically target drug-resistant bacteria
Natural PhiX174 runs into a wall against already resistant bacteria and cannot break through even after five passages; 16 AI-synthesised phages mixed together infected the originally resistant strain within one or two generations. Resistance is not broken by any single phage but by several synthetic phages recombining with each other and accumulating new mutations during replication, finally breaking the barrier through collective action. The result suggests that phage therapy should bet not on a single strain but on a cocktail of multiple synthetic phages.

1:07:29 Don't call AI-made viruses an urgent threat
For that study generating PhiX174, a contemporaneous commentary used the word "urgent" to describe its biosafety implications. Vincent directly rejected that wording on the show: the authors had already shown with reproducible experiments that this kind of research can be done safely, so what should be done is not to sound the alarm but to start building a safety framework. He also stressed that as long as you have enough sequence, reconstructing a virus is not science fiction — precisely why a framework is needed rather than fearmongering.

1:35:53 Not getting vaccinated is often just not knowing
Discussing the unvaccinated population, the article raises an often overlooked mechanism: some people do not get vaccinated not out of religious or ideological opposition but simply because they do not know they should. Treating vaccine hesitancy uniformly as a "matter of faith" gets the policy response wrong — for this group the key is not debate or persuasion but reaching them with information so they first know the vaccine exists.

item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-excessreturns-体育博彩渗透z世代-金融监管风险被低估/
