item.description: Inflation can't explain a 30-year above 5%: even with no inflation and no default risk, a buyer already full up on Treasuries at 5.3% won't budge for another $10 billion. What's really steepening the curve is $2 trillion of new supply a year, and the Treasury can't hold it down with buybacks either.
item.content:encoded:
Inflation can't explain a 30-year above 5%: even with no inflation and no default risk, a buyer already full up on Treasuries at 5.3% won't budge for another $10 billion. What's really steepening the curve is $2 trillion of new supply a year, and the Treasury can't hold it down with buybacks either.

The mainstream narrative pins the 30-year at 5% on inflation; this episode offers a genuinely additive alternative framework, folding the limits of Treasury intervention, the mechanics of Fed balance-sheet runoff, and the term premium debate into one logic.

4:04 5% is first a Treasury interest bill, not a macro signal
Host Joe asks Daryl what he sees when the 30-year Treasury yield is above 5% — even after it ticked down slightly that day following the Fed chair's remarks. Daryl's answer isn't a macro model but the Treasury's predicament: if I were the Treasury secretary, what I'd see is that US government interest expense is extraordinarily high, and I'd have to find a way to push yields down. That line sets the frame for the whole episode: the official side has a strong incentive to push long-end rates down, but whether it can and whether it should are the premises for everything that follows.

5:07 The Treasury wants to sell another $10 billion, it can only pay more
Daryl gives the single most important thought experiment of the segment: suppose there's no inflation risk and no sovereign default, and you're a macro hedge fund that already holds $20 billion of 10-year Treasuries. The Treasury secretary calls and asks you to buy another $10 billion — why won't you? The answer: at a 5.3% yield you've already made the allocation you want, and to get you to add, you'd have to be paid a higher interest rate as compensation. This logic incidentally explains the structural shift on the demand side — foreign central banks have long since filled their allocations and stopped buying, so new Treasury supply can only land on domestic free discretionary buyers: banks, pensions, insurers, hedge funds, and that money is highly sensitive to yield.

8:10 The logic didn't change, the debt hit a tipping point
Joe raises the objection that has to be faced: aging populations, a political system with no appetite for spending cuts, unsustainable deficits — this bearish logic existed in 2018 and 2019, and Japan was talked about this way for decades before that, so why did yields keep falling then and why are they rising now? Daryl's answer is a scale effect: the 60% debt-to-GDP red line the IMF drew back then is far behind us, France is already at 100%; the US Treasury market has grown from about $18 trillion to $31 trillion, and keeps expanding. There's no new logic — the quantity of debt itself has accumulated to a tipping point.

10:13 The long end's 5% is mostly issuance, not inflation expectations
Since the short end is still pinned by high inflation and the Fed, why not attribute the high 30-year yield directly to inflation expectations? Daryl concedes inflation over the past five years has indeed been well above the Fed's target and the job isn't done, but points out: implied inflation expectations backed out of real versus nominal bonds are not flashing alarm; the investors actually buying and selling 10-, 20- and 30-year Treasuries are not processing inflation first in their heads, but supply relative to demand. He mentions John Cochrane's fiscal theory of the price level, but that's a long-run framework — the main driver of today's term premium is issuance, not prices.

13:18 Buybacks to cap yields are just a signal, with far too little ammo
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced an expansion of Treasury buybacks, with the official rationale being liquidity. Daryl reads the subtext directly: from the wording of his public remarks, he doesn't think the problem is market liquidity, he thinks yields are ‘too high’, and he says outright that he's sending a signal to the market. The problem is that the size of Treasury's operations is a drop in the bucket relative to the whole Treasury market, and the market moved briefly on the news before reversing quickly. Trying to use the government's own resources to suppress the path of yields has a precedent in the 1992 sterling crisis — and Bessent was the man shorting the pound at Soros's fund back then.

19:22 Buybacks' real job is sweeping up old bonds, not managing rates
The original design of the buyback program was not to manage yields: as the Treasury keeps issuing new securities, a large stock of illiquid off-the-run old bonds is left in the market, clogging dealer balance sheets and pricing off a smooth yield curve. A paper Daryl is working on with two New York Fed economists is testing whether sweeping up the fragments on a ‘regular, predictable’ schedule and swapping in new issues can improve market liquidity and earn taxpayers the gain from buying low and selling high. The phrase ‘odd lots’ happens to be where the show's name comes from. He thinks this routine operation works; the Treasury stepping in at a moment of emergency to defend its own bond market is a different matter.

25:30 The runoff constraint is reserves, not the asset side
A new Fed chair wants to shrink the balance sheet, but most people only stare at the asset side. Daryl points to the arithmetic constraint: selling assets requires extinguishing an equal amount of liabilities. Of the three liability buckets, the TGA can't have the Treasury pull its deposits out, circulating cash can't be recalled, and the only thing that can be squeezed is commercial banks' reserves at the Fed. But today's reserves are ‘the Swiss Army knife of the financial industry’: they pay interest at market rates, satisfy liquidity regulation, and are ready for payments at any time, so banks have no incentive to give them up. The ratchet effect Acharya and Rajan laid out at Jackson Hole in 2017 already showed this: every time the Fed expands its balance sheet, banks get addicted to reserves, and shrinking it necessarily causes market volatility.

28:33 The task force will swap duration, not actually shrink the size
Daryl states he has no inside information on the task force, but makes two predictions about the group led by Jeremy Stein: first, the real problem isn't size but composition, and the sensible move is to gradually replace the Fed's long-term Treasuries with short-term bills, so that reserve interest expense on the liability side offsets bill interest income on the asset side, reducing the hit to the Fed's own P&L from policy-rate swings; second, don't keep mortgage-backed securities on the asset side — let them roll off naturally. His own conclusion is blunter: the Fed doesn't necessarily have to shrink the balance sheet, but it must have the tools in hand to shrink it on its own, or it will be backed into a corner when Congress applies pressure.

item.title: A wallet's profit engine isn't float interest, it's money moving inside the system
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-complexsys-钱包的利润密码不是余额利息-是钱在体系内流转/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-complexsys-钱包的利润密码不是余额利息-是钱在体系内流转/
item.description: The core ledger of a wallet: money coming in pays card-network tolls, internal transfers cost almost nothing, and money going out can be charged again. It earns the spread on flow, not interest on balances — and PayPal, Cash App and Stripe Link are all betting on that model.
item.content:encoded:
The core ledger of a wallet: money coming in pays card-network tolls, internal transfers cost almost nothing, and money going out can be charged again. It earns the spread on flow, not interest on balances — and PayPal, Cash App and Stripe Link are all betting on that model.

It takes the wallet cost structure apart for real: wholesale network pricing under ten cents, while platforms can charge users several times that; Japanese players even open accounts at multiple banks to route around clearing. Useful as a business teardown even if you don't do payments.

1:05 A wallet has to answer how it makes money on day one
It opens with a Venmo bill for $100 paid to his barber: for a small transaction that already has a mature payment rail, why does PayPal still want to wedge itself in and monetize it. Then it quickly sets the scope: this is about the e-wallet business, not crypto private-key wallets; because it appears to hold and disburse balances, it immediately enters the regulatory zone that treats deposits as sensitive, so a wallet has to answer how it makes money from the first day of design — if it can't, the product dies.

5:14 Card fraud isn't scammers building sites, it's issuer-side leaks
The biggest early obstacle to online transactions was that users didn't dare hand over their card numbers, and the media kept amplifying card-fraud risk. The author points out the opposite is true: most fraud comes from massive data leaks on the issuing side, not from scammers parasitizing checkout pages, and the conclusion is that "economies of scale protect criminals too." PayPal's value was standing between the user and the card number and the recipient, capping the risk of a single transaction — which gave it grounds to charge a toll near 3%, and planted the seed for the balance design that followed.

6:19 A free wallet is not free at all for the wallet
Putting money into a wallet goes through the card networks, at a historical list price of about 3%, and the wallet eats that cost; but once the balance stays inside the system, transfers between users amount to changing a row in a database, too cheap to bill for. PayPal charges close to full price on both the in and out ends, so simply substituting internal transfers for external ones adds a slice of gross margin. A wallet that is free to the average user is not free to the wallet — the zero marginal cost of the float is the real dam.

9:21 Driving down network fees beats product innovation for profit
There is no necessary relationship between wholesale and retail: buying millions of ACH transactions costs about $0.05 each, while a payment processor can quote a merchant close to $0.30; the spread is the tax the platform levies on the underlying plumbing. Japan is more extreme: interbank transfers cost about 200 yen per transaction while intra-bank entries are nearly free, so some products open accounts at each of the top banks, move the user's money inside the banks, and settle via daily netting. In finance, driving down network fees converts into wallet profit more directly than product innovation.

12:27 Cash-out isn't a user perk, it's a second toll pipe
Cash App prices cash-out the same way: want it fast and you pick the more expensive card rail, charged at 1.75% with a 25-cent minimum; the author tested withdrawing $50 and was quoted 88 cents. Paired with that is issuing prepaid cards through partners like Sutton Bank, so money spent outside the system still captures swipe fees. The wallet no longer treats cash-out as a user benefit but as a second revenue pipe, because the partner bank needs the wallet's user scale and the wallet needs the bank's issuing license.

20:53 On co-brand cards the wallet takes a cut and carries the bad debt
The logic of a wallet partnering on credit cards is charging both sides, but risk control is the real battlefield: wallets typically assume their accumulated spending data lets them underwrite more accurately than the issuing bank. The industry has repeatedly shown FICO is already strong enough to be hard to replace; the extra variables that could materially improve losses often cross legal red lines. What actually prices the wallet is the agreement — the bank requires the whole loan portfolio's loss rate to stay under a threshold, otherwise the wallet's revenue share goes to zero or it even pays in. The 10-K language dances around "loss sharing," but in essence the wallet is carrying the issuer's bad debt.

24:50 Users care about the phone, not the plastic card
Apple's core argument when negotiating with banks is that users care about the phone, not the plastic credit card; if banks won't pay, Apple can also back or build a new two-sided payment network and take users with it. The reported figure is that Apple takes 15 basis points per Apple Pay transaction, while Google reportedly takes nothing — the author uses this to gripe about the two giants' differing ability to do non-core products. The next layer is the conclusion that the checkout itself can be an ad slot: once the goods and price are fixed, who gets to rank a payment method first becomes a bidding war, and Stripe has already turned the traditional display into dynamic ordering by user preference, even opening up merchant fine-tuning options.

31:13 Network fees come down not at the table but in the defaults
Extend Link into a general-ledger-level settlement negotiation layer: if users store their low-cost payment methods in Link, the next checkout can bypass the card networks and go through bank accounts; the network fees saved get redistributed between merchants and users. This can't be negotiated by one company sitting at one table — it's the aggregation of decisions by millions of users and merchants, ultimately making the side it represents at the payments negotiating table approach 1% of global GDP. Only that kind of volume earns the right to reprice network fees.

item.title: If It Can't Solve Quantum Gravity, It Isn't Real AGI
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-spc-解不出量子引力-就不算真正的-agi/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-spc-解不出量子引力-就不算真正的-agi/
item.description: A physicist draws a high line for AGI: solving quantum gravity is what counts. The conversation also clarifies the real relationship between quantum materials and AI — materials found by search still have to pass the synthesizability gate, and the result may be zero.
item.content:encoded:
A physicist draws a high line for AGI: solving quantum gravity is what counts. The conversation also clarifies the real relationship between quantum materials and AI — materials found by search still have to pass the synthesizability gate, and the result may be zero.

A noise-reduction pass on the AI world's default assumptions: a string theorist makes the returns from science and the boundaries of AI concrete and checkable, useful for calibrating your own time expectations in hard tech. The narrative is a bit slow; the substance is concentrated in the middle and later sections.

17:28 Learning too much paralyzes you; only naivety dares ask the original questions
The hardest part of going from student to researcher isn't absorbing knowledge, it's posing the original questions that push the boundary of knowledge forward. Gopakumar describes this transition as ‘naivety plus experience’: learning too much can paralyze you, and you need to keep a bit of naivety to dare ask the questions that seem to have no way in; a mentor's job is to teach you to break a big problem into small steps you can advance right now without losing sight of the ultimate goal. His own advisor David Gross was very good at this — by his account, Gross's first student produced work that won the two of them a Nobel Prize together, and Witten also won a Fields Medal. Now he trains students by replicating the same method: the first one or two problems are assigned by him, and even he doesn't have the answers, and he stays with the student slowly working through them until the third or fourth year, when they start asking their own questions.

28:36 Spacetime isn't a background, it's an emergent approximation
Think of string theory through ‘water is made of discrete atoms’: the continuous spacetime we touch is very likely just a low-resolution approximation of some deeper structure at macroscopic scales. Gopakumar stresses this isn't pure speculation — quantum mechanics itself doesn't allow spacetime to be treated as an infinitely divisible smooth background; add black holes (Hawking and others found they have many anomalous properties) and the breakdown of the Big Bang at the singularity, and physicists have to answer ‘where does spacetime come from’. String theory happens to provide a natural framework: spacetime emerges from something more fundamental, and gravity and the known interactions fit inside it too. This explains why he treats ‘solving quantum gravity’ as a very high bar for intelligence: it demands not just the ability to solve problems, but the construction of new conceptual frameworks.

39:45 Materials should be designed backwards: set the property, then find the structure
Start with a long-horizon yardstick: quantum mechanics was originally just about understanding the atom, and the devices it now underpins account for roughly 35%-40% of US GDP by his estimate, while the commercial ripples only became obvious four or five decades after the theory appeared. He calls the current phase the second quantum revolution: quantum materials like graphene, found ‘by accident’, are already being commercialized, and the next step is inverse materials design with AI — first define what properties a material needs, then search for what structure can deliver them and how to synthesize it, bypassing traditional trial-and-error chemistry. He also reveals a conversation with Demis Hassabis: DeepMind's next holy grail is finding a room-temperature superconductor, and Hassabis told him from the start not to talk about quantum gravity.

50:59 Being stuck is the norm; keep three or four problems in the air at once
Being stuck isn't the exception, it's a researcher's daily life; especially in the student-to-researcher transition, being stuck can feel like a crush (being overwhelmed). Gopakumar's first strategy is portfolio hedging: push three or four problems at once, and when one dies, switch to another — probabilistically, one of them will move half a step. The second move is to go teach — the moment a student's eyes light up, that satisfaction can pull you out of a trough, and he has repeatedly found that ‘after a lecture, a stuck problem suddenly opens up’. The third move is to deliberately learn something new you've always wanted to learn but never had time for, to switch to a new frame of reference before returning to the old problem.

55:08 Talent is multiplicative, not additive; the shortage is never headcount
Why does top-tier science cluster in a few places rather than spreading evenly? Gopakumar gives the mechanism: talking in the same place, using each other as sounding boards, keeps the brain in a stimulated state even without formal collaboration; and once real collaboration happens, the different skills two people bring multiply rather than add. He borrows a physics metaphor: photons in an ordinary light bulb are chaotic, photons in a laser are coherent with each other, and a group of people that achieves coherence will also produce a lasing effect like a laser. He says many Indian institutions actually underperform relative to their talent, and what's missing isn't headcount but this resonant atmosphere; hence ICTS's founding principle is simple — hire only first-rate people, give them resources and freedom, and don't let them lower their ambitions.

1:11:19 AI can accelerate research, but it can't make conceptual leaps
AI just won two Nobel Prizes in a row, but Gopakumar splits ‘AI for science’ and ‘science for AI’ into two separate things: the former he grants is an overdrive gear, with AI accelerating a certain very narrow class of tasks in research; but the ‘theory’ AI does today is still far from his conceptual-layer standard, and the best physics relies on conceptual leaps rather than pattern recognition. Conversely, he's more bullish on science for AI — among the people who discovered scaling laws at Anthropic are those with physics backgrounds; Hopfield was himself a statistical physicist, using simple physical models to simulate the brain. Along this path, physicists may join computer scientists and neuroscientists to take AI from language models to physics-inspired world models. This distinction is worth remembering.

1:21:32 After the synthesizability gate, zero new AI materials remain
The soberest bucket of cold water in the whole session came from the audience Q&A: Google claims to have discovered a large number of new materials with AI, but after filtering out feasibility and the synthesizability gate, Gopakumar's phrasing is ‘I think left with zero’ — zero remain. His stance isn't to dismiss AI materials science (someone in the same session cited Microsoft's DFT model with only 385,000 parameters that bypasses traditional hybrid methods), but to remind that the whole chain is still long: after predicting a crystal structure you still have to grow it and scale it, and every step can filter out the surprises. He says India should also bet along this chain. The line is a useful reverse calibration for the ‘AI discovers new materials’ narrative.

item.title: AI's Frontrunners Are Just Refineries, Not the Native-App Winners
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-zhangxiaojun-ai没有安全巨头-公司制度将消亡/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-zhangxiaojun-ai没有安全巨头-公司制度将消亡/
item.description: AI has entered its agent phase: the first-stage leaders are only refineries, not the native-app winners; new platforms don't come from old platforms; organizations must shift from jobs to tasks; and in the end what people compete on is the creativity to make something out of nothing.
item.content:encoded:
AI has entered its agent phase: the first-stage leaders are only refineries, not the native-app winners; new platforms don't come from old platforms; organizations must shift from jobs to tasks; and in the end what people compete on is the creativity to make something out of nothing.

Zeng Ming gives you a coordinate system for judging where AI sits, using a three-stage industrial history — an antidote to the optimism of "this time is different," plus the opportunity window for application founders and a brutal forecast for incumbents' transformation.

16:28 Building agents today is like building websites in 1992
Zeng Ming divides the industrialization of a general-purpose technology into three stages: first it becomes social infrastructure, then applications explode, and finally native applications appear. In 2026, token as a unit of measure reaching consensus shows the first stage has matured; the agent events around Chinese New Year (commonly called "lobster") mark AI's formal entry into the agent stage. He draws the analogy to the 1992 website-building movement: back then people built websites to share information, today they build agents to share capabilities. The browser hasn't appeared yet, and whoever can establish the agent standard and seize the user entry point may hold the biggest opportunity of the next two years.

27:49 A ten-trillion-dollar company will appear, but not these two
Zeng Ming says plainly that OpenAI and Anthropic are remarkable technological and commercial achievements, but business history shows the first wave of breakout companies is most likely not the big winners of the native-application stage. Yahoo reached a $120 billion market cap five years after founding, AOL was valued at $220 billion, and neither became the Google of the next era. Model companies are more like AI cloud companies, refineries that refine crude oil — the real application value belongs to chemical plants and car companies, and cars were not built by oil companies. He believes a ten-trillion-dollar company will certainly exist in the future, but it may not be the two current frontrunners. Model companies will evolve into a mature business of oligopoly plus heavy government regulation.

1:10:29 The unit of an AI-native organization is the task, not the job
The company corresponds to the hierarchical bureaucracy of the industrial age; AI overturns the industrial age, and the corporate system will die out. The basic unit of an AI-native organization is not the job but the task: people are not organized by reporting lines but flow around "what needs to be solved," and humans and AI coordinate around tasks. So well-designed jobs and hierarchies will disappear, and the traditional middle layer will die out too; future founders must first define the organization's task network. Silicon Valley's NewLab is a prototype of the new organizational form, and OpenAI itself looks more like a Lab than a traditional company. The culture of the new organization is more like a sports team, emphasizing transparency, sharing and co-creation, no longer relying on commands and performance reviews.

1:31:32 Excellence can only be judged afterward; being good is visible on the spot
Zeng Ming argues that "good ≠ great." Being good is growth that keeps getting positive feedback, while greatness requires overcoming negative feedback again and again, persisting when everyone disapproves, and finally proving through enormous success that you were the era's prophet — which is why "greatness is judged after the fact." Good people easily fall into a cycle of proving themselves, which makes their strategies conservative. Great people have a small ego, tend to attribute success to the times and their partners, and are driven by mission rather than external valuation. When identifying founders he asks, "Ten years from now, what kind of self would you be satisfied with?" If the answer is "building a ten-billion-dollar company," that is mainly ego-driven, not an inner mission. Truly great founders tend to be altruistic and empathetic.

1:47:24 Strategy in the AI era can't be planned, only generated
Strategy in the AI era is not planning but generation. Zeng Ming proposes a "strategy generation system": the organization must build an environment and network in which strategic insight emerges naturally. Because decision frequency is higher and quality demands are higher, a CEO cannot plan by linear extrapolation, nor can strategy be outsourced to McKinsey — McKinsey's explosion was a product of the slow maturity of the industrial age. His methodology is "look ten years out, think three years out, act one year out," with the core being "think three years out": you must at least see two or three milestones so that short-term action creates tension with the mid-term picture. Organization-building must guarantee enough context rather than control, letting the right people make the right decisions at the right time.

2:01:39 The right analogy for robots is appliances, not cars
Zeng Ming believes robotics is still in a strategic exploration phase, far from convergence. Of the two current paths — build a general brain first or close the scenario loop first — both are logically valid, and it's impossible to judge in advance which is faster. By historical analogy, the auto industry had thousands of companies from 1900 to 1920, and only entered scale when Ford built the assembly line in 1913; robots have yet to reach their Model T moment, and whoever actually sells ten thousand robots first is already remarkable. But the better analogy for robots is appliances rather than cars: after electricity was invented came countless categories — refrigerators, washing machines, air conditioners — and robots interacting in the physical world will have N kinds of big scenarios; home, companionship and industry could each produce their own native giant.

2:03:39 The incumbents who feel safe are the least safe
Zeng Ming says that in the face of a giant wave no one is safe, and feeling safe is the most unsafe thing of all. In business history, no era's companies have ever transitioned smoothly into the next era; IBM and Microsoft are the only two possible exceptions, and both are full of uncertainty. AI is a productivity revolution that overturns the industrial revolution, not a continuity innovation like mobile internet, so old giants' technology reserves and organizational culture are negative assets. Google can live on as an AI cloud company but may not capture the consumer entry point; ByteDance has an AI cloud opportunity, but Doubao is not the future application; Tencent's social relationships will be restructured; Alibaba is likewise not naturally safe. The new platform will most likely be created by a new company.

2:20:56 Human value lies in making something from nothing, not writing songs or painting
Borrowing Drucker's framework, Zeng Ming defines the AI era as the era of creativity: all knowledge work that can be structured will be taken over by AI, and people are on one hand forced and on the other finally liberated to develop new potential. That potential is called creativity — not writing songs or painting, but the ability to originally define complex problems and make something out of nothing. AI has already taken away all existing knowledge; human value lies in creating what does not yet exist. That is why he calls his mission "being a happy researcher," and believes civilization's next step will reorganize around creativity, forcing even the education system to shift from "knowledge indoctrination" to "open exploration," because young people already know the old path leads nowhere.

item.title: The moat in AI writing isn't the model, it's the proprietary data you feed it
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-aiandi-ai-写作的护城河不是模型-而是你喂进去的独家数据/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-aiandi-ai-写作的护城河不是模型-而是你喂进去的独家数据/
item.description: Every writer Katie spent two years turning ChatGPT from a career coach during a layoff into a one-person content company and a compounding editor; the core method isn't prompts, it's using proprietary experience to cover the "last mile" the model can't reach.
item.content:encoded:
Every writer Katie spent two years turning ChatGPT from a career coach during a layoff into a one-person content company and a compounding editor; the core method isn't prompts, it's using proprietary experience to cover the "last mile" the model can't reach.

Not a tool review, but how a non-technical writer uses AI as a mode of production: the substance is concentrated in the last 30 minutes, and the personal story up front supplies the motivation and context.

2:09 The biggest value of an AI coach isn't saving money
After being laid off she was at a low point and couldn't afford a human career coach's hourly rate, but a $20-a-month ChatGPT subscription was acceptable. She found that writing her thoughts out and letting AI question and push back from the outside helped her externalise her thinking, fight catastrophising, and gave her a sense of accountability. The most important legacy of that experience wasn't the money saved, but that it made her believe AI really can drive concrete change in a life. At the time she was hesitating over whether to take Every's freelance offer, and it was ChatGPT that gave her the push to just try it.

8:26 Throughput comes from upfront context, not clever prompts
She once took on a delivery load of 8 blog posts, 3 ebooks, 24 LinkedIn posts, 24 X posts and 16 Instagram posts in a week and a half. She could do it not because she knew a smarter one-line prompt, but because she did a great deal of upfront context engineering: feeding the model brand information, product details, audience profiles and differentiators all at once. Much of the demand was essentially content repurposing, and AI is good at rewriting one long piece into versions for different platforms. The rule she distilled: set the scene up front, and only then can you move fast later.

11:28 Give the model a fence first, then talk tone and word choice
Before Claude Projects existed, she could only keep persistent documents in Google Docs and manually copy-paste them into context each time. This structure didn't fall from the sky; it comes from the style guide tradition in content marketing: first define who the audience is, what the pain points are, how the product maps to them, who the competitors are and where the differentiation lies. She says this amounts to giving the model a playground with a fence: first make sure it won't wander off, then talk about word choice, tone and reading difficulty. Later, as soon as Projects launched, she built a separate project for every client and every column.

15:40 The last mile of AI writing can only be covered by a human
She believes AI writing has a "last mile" problem: the model has a knowledge cutoff, and it isn't in the real physical world. So the human's job is to supply the latest data and real experience that AI can't reach. She warns that if you just throw the model one line — "write a blog post about style guides" — all you get is the generic content it already knows, which is commoditised information; what actually makes writing unique is the fresh ingredients the model has never seen: internal company research, third-party reports, personal experience. The writing system is the kitchen; the human is responsible for supplying good ingredients.

22:50 AI's value is reducing friction, not speeding up output
She talks openly about her bipolar disorder and points out that AI's value isn't just producing content faster, but reducing friction in life. She put off booking a primary care doctor for three years, and eventually just had Codex find doctors who accept her insurance and are taking new patients and complete the booking; email is first filtered by automation, and only messages that genuinely need a human reply reach her inbox. She says this completely solved her email anxiety. This isn't treating AI as a production tool but as assistive technology, making her day-to-day running "as a person" easier.

27:03 Let AI interview you repeatedly, and it can prioritise for you
Two years ago she merely asked ChatGPT whether it could be her career coach; today that coach lives in a Codex project containing her job profile, Every's brand positioning, content performance data, a folder of reader praise and her OKRs. She doesn't maintain the board herself; she uses voice conversation to have the system prioritise by highest impact, and the system maintains her Kanban for her. The key to building this system was letting AI interview her repeatedly and then sedimenting those interviews into context. She says it's like having a Chief of Staff, not just a writer.

32:27 Feedback that only fixes the current draft is wasted
The core of the Compound Writing plugin is compounding thinking: every piece of feedback given to AI should flow back into the system so the next output is automatically better. She forked Kieran Klassen's Compound Engineering plugin and adapted it into a writing workflow: code and writing both have brainstorming, planning, drafting and review stages, except writing focuses more on structure, voice and evidence. Editing is further split into a substantive edit that looks at big structure and argument, a line edit that works sentence by sentence, and a final pass that checks before publication. Now she doesn't write in a web chat window, but feeds the day's fresh material into this system.

39:19 Vonnegut as editor gives you a perspective, not a verdict
She built Vonnegut's eight narrative elements, Hitchcock's principle of suspense about the bomb under the table, and the expressive styles of Sorkin and Sedaris into the plugin as editing skills. Vonnegut checks whether "the story starts as close to the end as possible" and whether "every sentence earns its place"; Hitchcock's perspective asks whether the reader will want to keep reading because of this. She stresses that this isn't letting the masters' ghosts mark up your draft, but giving you a new perspective you can accept or reject; non-professional writers may actually benefit more, because they're less likely to be picking at themselves while they write.

item.title: Stronger Models Make Dirty Data Deadlier: Cleaning Is Worth More, Not Less
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-signalsandthre-模型越强-脏数据越致命-清洗反而更值钱/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-signalsandthre-模型越强-脏数据越致命-清洗反而更值钱/
item.description: Jane Street's alternative data team found that once data leaks future information into the past, the stronger the model the more dangerous it gets; pinning down what was known at the time is worth more than tuning the model.
item.content:encoded:
Jane Street's alternative data team found that once data leaks future information into the past, the stronger the model the more dangerous it gets; pinning down what was known at the time is worth more than tuning the model.

This episode is a dense account of how data engineering actually creates value; the second half, on corrected data, timestamps and cost models, contains judgments you won't hear in most AI discussions.

2:06 Once a pattern is found, competition erases it
This is what Eric defines as an anti-inductive environment: in trading, the patterns you find tend to be quickly absorbed by other people and the market, and then stop working; very little knowledge can be accumulated over the long term the way physical laws can. For the same reason, the signal-to-noise ratio of trading data is naturally ugly — the whole mechanism of the market is to keep squeezing out extractable signal, and what's left gets closer and closer to a random walk. To keep winning, you have to keep finding new facts rather than guarding old patterns.

19:21 Prices can go negative, so don't hard-code assumptions into the system
On April 20, 2020, the settlement price of near-expiry crude oil futures on the CME closed negative — just for that one day, and the final settlement price later returned to positive. The reason wasn't that oil had no value, but that storage space at the delivery point, Cushing, was nearly full and nobody wanted to take physical delivery. Order and risk systems that had long assumed prices must be positive failed on the spot: some people couldn't place orders, others didn't know how to handle negative returns. Eric's conclusion is that a large part of trading is understanding the boring details of reality: tank capacity, contract multipliers, quote units. Only when the system gets these details right can you draw a ceiling on risk.

32:33 Domain experts don't know how good good tools can be
For data and systems to be genuinely usable, the bottleneck is often not writing code but translation. Eric observes that traders have a high tolerance for painful workflows, ground down by Excel and manual processes to the point where they don't know they deserve better tools; conversely, software engineers who don't understand the trading domain can only build to a narrow spec. So his job is to explain the domain's real mechanics to engineers, and to explain how good things could be to traders. Jane Street now has such an embedded developer on every desk, and that role originally grew out of exactly this.

59:04 The number of parking spaces is not the sales figure
The classic example of alternative data is counting cars in a Walmart parking lot, where more people in cars means better business. Eric says this example is actually terrible: what you want to infer is consumer spending, but parking spaces only tell you foot traffic, very indirectly; about 20% of Walmart's shopping happens online, and a city like New York has no parking lots to count. The more direct signal is on the transaction side: issuing banks, the Visa/Mastercard networks, and credit union processing systems know how much people actually spent, and can sell anonymised aggregate statistics to buyers.

1:04:08 Corrected data turns a backtest into a time machine
When deciding whether to subscribe to a dataset, the vendor may already have corrected past errors; backtesting on the pretty corrected data doesn't test what you would actually have received at the time, but the right answer you only learned later. Eric says this is equivalent to simulating that you have a time machine. Jane Street's solution is to keep every piece of raw data and the local timestamp at which it was received, so that no matter how many transformations you do later, you can reconstruct what we actually knew at that moment. This is the same logic as distrusting exchange timestamps and trusting only your own data's arrival time.

1:08:10 LLMs know the future, so keep them off historical data
AI hits alternative data on two levels: stronger predictive models raise the value of good data, and LLMs also make it easy to extract features from text. But watch out for a causal trap — using the latest LLM to featurize old documents drags in what happened later: it knows how Enron ended, and it may have seen later revisions of this financial report in its training data. This amounts to creating a new leak of future information, and when handling historical data you especially need to pin down which point-in-time model you're using.

1:11:26 The stronger the model, the more data cleaning is worth
A common expectation is that as neural networks get stronger, feature engineering and manual cleaning will be replaced. Eric's view is the opposite: once models can do more on their own, you can do less manual feature work, but the data you feed in has to be more correct. If the data isn't point-in-time and quietly leaks future information into the past, stronger models will learn that problem; different models also have different tolerances for outliers and patches of dirty data. All told, cleaning data is worth more, not less.

1:16:34 Usage-based billing pushes teams to keep saving money
Jane Street runs its data warehouse in its own machine room, and it isn't purely about control. Eric's observation is that moving the same queries to a cloud vendor billed by reads or compute time gets expensive enough that you feel "this money would buy a pile of hardware". More important is the distorting effect of the cost model — usage-based billing makes teams constantly optimise the bill and reshape workloads to accommodate the billing; once you build your own, cost becomes a one-off hardware investment, and the team spends its time on research and queries themselves rather than on saving money.

item.title: The most valuable step in writing with AI isn't the prompt — it's compounding your revision feedback
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-every-用-ai-写作最值钱的一步不是提示词-而是把改稿反馈沉淀成复利/
